notes:
1. Inter-State Comparison — Purpose

  • Indian States differ in population, geography, natural resources, urbanisation, industrialisation, fiscal capacity, education, health and demographic transition.
  • Tamil Nadu's development is best understood by comparing it with other major States across comparable indicators.
  • The purpose is to identify relative strengths and weaknesses, not to declare one State universally superior.
📌 Must-Memorise

Inter-State Comparison → Compare Dimensions, Not Just Rankings

2. Golden Rule of State Comparison

Valid comparisons should use:

  • Census with the same Census year.
  • PLFS with the same reference year and definition.
  • NFHS with the same NFHS round.
  • SRS with the corresponding period.
  • AISHE with the same academic year.
  • NITI indices with the same edition.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Different Years + Different Sources → Invalid Direct Comparison

3. Census, Projection and Index Data

  • Census count → Actual official enumeration.
  • Projection → Statistical estimate.
  • MPI → Multidimensional deprivation.
  • SDG Index → Sustainable-development performance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Census ≠ Projection

MPI ≠ Monetary Poverty

SDG Score ≠ HDI

4. Tamil Nadu — Overall Development Character

Tamil Nadu combines:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Services.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Higher education.
  • Public-health development.
  • Social welfare.
  • Low multidimensional poverty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Model → Social Development + Manufacturing + Services + Urbanisation

5. Tamil Nadu — Balanced Development Structure

  • Tamil Nadu does not lead India in every indicator.
  • Its distinctive strength is balance across economic and social dimensions.
  • Kerala performs better in several classic social indicators.
  • Gujarat is more industry-intensive.
  • Karnataka has strong technology-led services.
  • Maharashtra has larger overall economic scale.

6. Per Capita GSDP — Tamil Nadu

According to the cited NITI Aayog comparison:

  • Tamil Nadu nominal per capita GSDP in 2021–22 → approximately ₹2.71 lakh.
  • Corresponding all-India level → approximately ₹1.71 lakh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Per Capita GSDP → Above National Level

7. Per Capita Income — Interpretation

Per capita output indicates average economic capacity.

It does not directly show:

  • Income distribution.
  • Poverty.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Human development.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Per Capita Income ≠ Human Development

8. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — Income Capacity

  • Kerala also has high per capita economic capacity.
  • Tamil Nadu and Kerala differ more strongly in economic structure than in broad average economic capability.

9. Tamil Nadu vs Gujarat — Income Comparison Caution

  • The source cites Gujarat's nominal per capita income at about ₹3,36,875 in 2023–24.
  • Tamil Nadu's cited figure is from 2021–22.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Do Not Directly Rank Two Rupee Values from Different Years

10. Tamil Nadu vs Bihar — Economic Gap

  • Bihar's per capita economic output is far below Tamil Nadu's.
  • The gap reflects differences in:
  • Productivity.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Human capital.
  • Employment structure.

11. Tamil Nadu — Economic Structure

According to the cited 2021–22 profile, Tamil Nadu GSVA was approximately:

  • Services → 53.0%.
  • Industry → 33.9%.
  • Agriculture → 13.2%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Services Largest + Strong Industry

12. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — Economic Structure

  • Kerala is more strongly service-oriented.
  • Services accounted for roughly 64% of Kerala's State value added in the corresponding framework.
  • Tamil Nadu has a substantially larger industrial base.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kerala → More Service-Dominated

Tamil Nadu → Stronger Manufacturing Depth

13. Tamil Nadu vs Gujarat — Economic Structure

  • Gujarat represents a more industry-intensive model.
  • The source reports an industry share of about 48.1% of GSVA in 2023–24.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gujarat → Higher Industrial Intensity than Tamil Nadu

14. Tamil Nadu vs Karnataka — Economic Structure

  • Karnataka has a strong service-led economy.
  • Its major comparative advantage is information technology and other knowledge-intensive services.
  • Tamil Nadu has greater manufacturing depth.

15. Tamil Nadu — Manufacturing Share

  • Manufacturing accounted for approximately 19.7% of Tamil Nadu GSVA in 2021–22.
  • The all-India share in the cited profile was about 14.8%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Manufacturing Share → Above National Level

16. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — Manufacturing

  • Tamil Nadu manufacturing → about 19.7% of GSVA.
  • Kerala manufacturing → roughly 9% in the corresponding comparison.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Much Stronger Manufacturing Base than Kerala

17. Tamil Nadu — Major Industrial Ecosystems

Important sectors include:

  • Automobiles.
  • Auto components.
  • Textiles.
  • Garments.
  • Leather.
  • Engineering.
  • Electronics.
  • Chemicals.
  • Cement.
  • Food processing.

18. Manufacturing — Employment Linkages

Tamil Nadu's manufacturing base supports indirect employment through:

  • Logistics.
  • Warehousing.
  • Engineering services.
  • Repair.
  • Transport.
  • Business services.

19. Urbanisation — Tamil Nadu

  • Census 2011 urban population share → approximately 48.4%.
  • Projected 2023 urban share in the cited profile → approximately 53.7%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

48.4% → Census

53.7% → Projection

20. Tamil Nadu — Polycentric Urban Pattern

Major urban-industrial centres include:

  • Chennai.
  • Coimbatore.
  • Madurai.
  • Tiruchirappalli.
  • Salem.
  • Tiruppur.
  • Erode.
  • Hosur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Urbanisation → Multiple Major Centres, Not Chennai Alone

21. Tamil Nadu vs Karnataka — Urban Structure

  • Karnataka has major urban concentration around Bengaluru.
  • Tamil Nadu has a more distributed network of large industrial and service centres.

22. Tamil Nadu vs Bihar — Urbanisation

  • Tamil Nadu is highly urbanised.
  • Bihar remains predominantly rural in the cited projection framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu–Bihar Contrast → Urban-Industrial vs Predominantly Rural Structure

23. Census 2011 Literacy — Major-State Comparison

Comparable Census 2011 literacy rates:

  • Kerala → 94.0%.
  • Maharashtra → 82.3%.
  • Tamil Nadu → 80.1%.
  • Gujarat → 78.0%.
  • Karnataka → 75.4%.
  • Bihar → 61.8%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kerala Highest Among These Comparators

Tamil Nadu → 80.1%

24. Literacy — Tamil Nadu's Position

  • Tamil Nadu was above the national Census 2011 literacy level.
  • It remained below Kerala and Maharashtra among the cited comparators.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tamil Nadu ≠ Highest Literacy State

25. Literacy vs Learning Quality

  • Literacy measures a basic threshold.
  • It does not measure:
  • Numeracy.
  • School-learning quality.
  • Higher-order skills.
  • Employability.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Literacy ≠ Learning Quality

26. Higher-Education GER — Tamil Nadu

  • AISHE 2021–22 data cited by NITI Aayog place Tamil Nadu's higher-education GER at approximately 47% for ages 18–23.
  • The all-India GER in the same comparison was 28.4%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Higher-Education GER → \~47%

All India → 28.4%

27. Tamil Nadu — Higher-Education Comparative Strength

  • Tamil Nadu was identified in the cited analysis as the leading large State in higher-education GER.
  • This is one of Tamil Nadu's clearest comparative strengths.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Major Strength in Higher-Education Participation

28. Industrial Strength vs Higher-Education GER

  • Gujarat has stronger industrial intensity.
  • Tamil Nadu has much higher higher-education participation in the cited comparison.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Industrial Strength ≠ Automatically High Higher-Education GER

29. Life Expectancy — Comparable SRS 2020

Approximate values:

  • Kerala → 75 years.
  • Tamil Nadu → 73.2 years.
  • Maharashtra → 72.9 years.
  • All India → about 70 years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kerala > Tamil Nadu > National Level

30. Life Expectancy — Interpretation

Life expectancy reflects combined effects of:

  • Nutrition.
  • Income.
  • Public health.
  • Medical care.
  • Education.
  • Sanitation.
  • Maternal and child health.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Economic Output Alone ≠ Highest Life Expectancy

31. Infant Mortality Rate — SRS 2020

Comparable values per 1,000 live births:

  • Kerala → 6.
  • Tamil Nadu → 13.
  • Maharashtra → 16.
  • Karnataka → 19.
  • All India → about 28.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lower IMR = Better Performance

32. Tamil Nadu — IMR Position

  • Tamil Nadu performed substantially better than the national level.
  • Kerala performed better than Tamil Nadu.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tamil Nadu ≠ Best Among All States on IMR

33. Why IMR Is a Strong Comparison Indicator

IMR reflects:

  • Maternal care.
  • Institutional delivery.
  • Newborn care.
  • Immunisation.
  • Nutrition.
  • Sanitation.
  • Primary-health access.

34. Fertility — NFHS-5 Comparison

Approximate TFR values:

  • Tamil Nadu → 1.8.
  • Kerala → 1.8.
  • Karnataka → 1.7.
  • Maharashtra → 1.7.
  • Gujarat → about 1.9.
  • Bihar → about 3.0.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Low Fertility, Advanced Demographic Transition

35. Fertility — Development Interpretation

  • Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Maharashtra are further through demographic transition than Bihar.
  • Low fertility eventually contributes to population ageing.

36. Different Demographic Challenges

More advanced-transition States:

  • Ageing.
  • Elderly care.
  • Labour supply.
  • Social security.

Younger States:

  • Education.
  • Skills.
  • Maternal-child health.
  • Job creation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Different Demographic Stage → Different Policy Priority

37. Multidimensional Poverty — 2019–21

NITI Aayog MPI headcount ratios:

  • Kerala → 0.55%.
  • Tamil Nadu → 2.20%.
  • Karnataka → 7.58%.
  • Maharashtra → 7.81%.
  • Gujarat → 11.66%.
  • Uttar Pradesh → 22.93%.
  • Bihar → 33.76%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu MPI → Very Low, but Kerala Lower

38. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — MPI

  • Kerala → 0.55%.
  • Tamil Nadu → 2.20%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Kerala Performs Better than Tamil Nadu on MPI

39. Tamil Nadu vs Industrial Peers — MPI

Tamil Nadu's MPI was lower than:

  • Karnataka.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Gujarat.
📌 Must-Memorise

High Income/Industry ≠ Automatically Lowest MPI

40. Tamil Nadu vs Bihar — MPI Contrast

  • Tamil Nadu → 2.20%.
  • Bihar → 33.76%.
  • This reflects large differences in education, nutrition, basic services and living conditions.

41. Employment Structure — Tamil Nadu

According to cited PLFS 2022–23 data:

  • Agriculture, forestry and fishing → 28.9%.
  • Manufacturing → 16.8%.
  • Construction → 18.0%.
  • Services → 35.2%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Workforce → Less Agriculture-Dependent than Several Major States

42. Tamil Nadu vs Karnataka — Agricultural Employment

  • Tamil Nadu → about 28.9% workers in agriculture.
  • Karnataka → roughly 46% in the same broad reference period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Karnataka Tech Strength ≠ Lower Agricultural Employment than Tamil Nadu

43. Tamil Nadu — Structural Transformation

Tamil Nadu's employment pattern shows movement towards:

Agriculture

→ Manufacturing

  • Construction
  • Services
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Comparatively Advanced Employment-Side Structural Transformation

44. Tamil Nadu — Unemployment Rate

  • The cited PLFS 2022–23 profile gives Tamil Nadu an unemployment rate of approximately 4.3%.
  • The corresponding national figure was about 3.2%.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

More Diversified Economy ≠ Automatically Lowest Unemployment Rate

45. Employment Quality — Comparison Principle

A good employment structure requires more than low unemployment.

Important factors include:

  • Productivity.
  • Wages.
  • Job security.
  • Social protection.
  • Skill matching.

46. Gender Development — Multidimensional Nature

Gender development should be assessed using:

  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Maternal health.
  • Sex ratio.
  • Political participation.
  • Economic independence.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

One Gender Indicator ≠ Complete Gender Equality

47. Tamil Nadu — Female Higher-Education Strength

  • Tamil Nadu performs strongly in female higher-education participation.
  • Its higher-education Gender Parity Index was above 1 in the cited reference period.

48. Tamil Nadu — Sex Ratio at Birth Caution

According to the cited NFHS-5 comparison:

  • Tamil Nadu sex ratio at birth → approximately 878 female births per 1,000 male births.
  • All India → approximately 929.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Performs Strongly in Some Gender Indicators, Not All

49. Gujarat — Sex Ratio at Birth Comparison

  • The source reports Gujarat at approximately 955 under the cited NFHS-5 measure.
  • This was above the corresponding national estimate.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Overall Census Sex Ratio ≠ Sex Ratio at Birth

50. Tamil Nadu — Basic Amenities

NFHS-5 indicators cited:

  • Improved drinking-water source → 98.6%.
  • Electricity access → 99.0%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Very High Basic-Service Access in Cited Indicators

51. Basic Service Access vs Quality

  • Access to an improved source does not guarantee continuous supply, adequate quantity or service quality.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Infrastructure Access ≠ Service Quality

52. SDG India Index — 2023–24

Scores in the same edition:

  • Kerala → 79.
  • Tamil Nadu → 78.
  • All India → 71.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu SDG Score → 78

53. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — SDG Performance

  • Kerala scored one point higher than Tamil Nadu.
  • Both performed substantially above the national score.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

78 → SDG Index Score, Not HDI

54. Tamil Nadu vs Kerala — Core Contrast

Kerala:

  • Higher literacy.
  • Higher life expectancy.
  • Lower IMR.
  • Lower MPI.
  • More service-oriented economy.

Tamil Nadu:

  • Stronger manufacturing base.
  • Very high higher-education participation.
  • Diversified industry + services structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kerala → Classic Social Outcomes

Tamil Nadu → Social Development + Manufacturing Depth

55. Tamil Nadu vs Karnataka — Core Contrast

Karnataka:

  • Strong IT and knowledge-services economy.
  • Higher agricultural employment share in cited data.

Tamil Nadu:

  • Stronger manufacturing orientation.
  • Lower agricultural employment dependence.
  • More advanced employment-side structural transformation.

56. Tamil Nadu vs Maharashtra — Core Contrast

Maharashtra:

  • Larger total economy.
  • Major finance and service centre.
  • Census literacy slightly above Tamil Nadu.

Tamil Nadu:

  • Stronger cited higher-education participation.
  • Lower SRS IMR in the cited 2020 comparison.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Larger Total GSDP ≠ Better Per Capita or Human Development Automatically

57. Tamil Nadu vs Gujarat — Core Contrast

Gujarat:

  • Higher industrial intensity.
  • Strong manufacturing orientation.

Tamil Nadu:

  • Stronger cited higher-education participation.
  • Better cited longevity outcomes.
  • Lower multidimensional poverty in 2019–21.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gujarat → Industrial Intensity

Tamil Nadu → More Balanced Social + Industrial Outcomes

58. Tamil Nadu vs Bihar — Development-Stage Contrast

Tamil Nadu:

  • Literacy → 80.1%.
  • TFR → about 1.8.
  • MPI → 2.20%.
  • Highly urbanised and industrialised.

Bihar:

  • Literacy → 61.8%.
  • TFR → about 3.0.
  • MPI → 33.76%.
  • Predominantly rural in the cited framework.

59. Why Tamil Nadu and Bihar Need Different Policies

Tamil Nadu increasingly requires:

  • Elderly care.
  • Urban infrastructure.
  • Employment quality.
  • Skill matching.
  • Advanced health services.

Bihar and similar younger States require especially large investments in:

  • Basic education.
  • Nutrition.
  • Maternal-child health.
  • Job creation.
  • Basic infrastructure.

60. Tamil Nadu — Distinctive Comparative Strength

Tamil Nadu performs particularly strongly in the combination of:

  • Higher education.
  • Manufacturing.
  • Low multidimensional poverty.
  • Health outcomes.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu's Distinctive Advantage → Economic Diversification + Social Development

61. Comparison Memory Chain — Kerala

Kerala:

  • Literacy → 94%.
  • Life expectancy → \~75.
  • IMR → 6.
  • MPI → 0.55%.
  • SDG score → 79.
  • Strong service economy.

62. Comparison Memory Chain — Tamil Nadu

Tamil Nadu:

  • Literacy → 80.1%.
  • Life expectancy → 73.2.
  • IMR → 13.
  • MPI → 2.20%.
  • Higher-ed GER → \~47%.
  • Manufacturing share → 19.7%.
  • SDG score → 78.

63. Comparison Memory Chain — Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra

  • Gujarat → Highest industrial intensity among these cited comparisons.
  • Karnataka → Technology and knowledge services.
  • Maharashtra → Large diversified economy + finance.
  • Tamil Nadu → Manufacturing + services + social development.

64. Comparison Memory Chain — Bihar and Uttar Pradesh

  • Bihar MPI → 33.76%.
  • Uttar Pradesh MPI → 22.93%.
  • Tamil Nadu MPI → 2.20%.
  • Younger demographic structures imply different development priorities.

65. TNPSC Traps

  • Tamil Nadu is not the best-performing State in every indicator.
  • Kerala performs better in literacy, life expectancy, IMR and MPI in the cited data.
  • Tamil Nadu has stronger manufacturing depth than Kerala.
  • Gujarat has a higher industrial share than Tamil Nadu.
  • Karnataka's technology leadership does not mean lower agricultural employment.
  • Maharashtra's larger total economy does not automatically mean stronger human development.
  • Total GSDP and per capita GSDP are different.
  • Per capita income and HDI are different.
  • High income does not automatically mean low MPI.
  • Tamil Nadu MPI is lower than Karnataka, Maharashtra and Gujarat in 2019–21.
  • Kerala MPI is lower than Tamil Nadu's.
  • Census data and projections must not be mixed.
  • Literacy and higher-education GER measure different things.
  • Tamil Nadu's higher-education GER is a major comparative strength.
  • GER does not measure quality.
  • Lower IMR is better.
  • Life expectancy and IMR measure different health outcomes.
  • TFR is not population growth rate.
  • Low fertility contributes to ageing.
  • Urbanisation does not automatically guarantee human development.
  • Low unemployment does not automatically mean high-quality employment.
  • Tamil Nadu's economy can be diversified while its unemployment rate remains above some comparators.
  • Overall sex ratio and sex ratio at birth are different.
  • Tamil Nadu performs strongly on female higher education but not on every gender indicator.
  • SDG score and HDI are different.
  • Tamil Nadu's 78 is an SDG India Index score.
  • State comparisons should use comparable sources and years.
  • Inter-State comparison should not be reduced to political ranking.
